title: The Export Control Precedent
publicBriefing: Three days after a frontier AI lab launched its most capable model, the US Commerce Department issued an emergency export control directive ordering immediate suspension of access for all foreign nationals, citing national security. Unable to filter users by nationality in real time, the company disabled the model for everyone worldwide. Hundreds of millions of users and thousands of enterprise customers lost access overnight. The company says the cited vulnerability is narrow and exists in competitor models. The government hasn't made its evidence public.
stakes: This is the first time a government has used export controls to kill-switch a commercial AI model. Whatever precedent is set here applies to every frontier model that follows.
designNote: This scenario tests decision-making under genuine uncertainty. Key facts are contested, evidence is secret, and actors must commit before knowing what's actually true. The contested intel mechanic forces players to decide what they believe, not just what they know.

bullets: Your directive was issued based on a tip from a competing AI company that the model could be jailbroken to unlock autonomous cybersecurity capabilities. The tip included a proof-of-concept. Your technical team assessed it as credible but has not independently reproduced it.

[CONTESTED] Intelligence suggests a China-linked group accessed the model through a large-scale account fraud operation. Approximately 25,000 fraudulent accounts conducted 28.8 million exchanges over 6 weeks, potentially extracting enough capability to reverse-engineer core functionality. The lab reported this separately but says it was unrelated to the export control decision.

Your legal authority for this action is untested. You used emergency export control powers in a way that has never been applied to a software API before. Legal scholars are split on whether this survives judicial review. The company is already suing the administration on separate grounds.

Three allied nations have privately expressed concern that the precedent applies to their own AI companies. The UK and Canada have asked for advance consultation before any future actions. A senior White House advisor publicly stated the government acted on the jailbreak report, implying the company was warned and failed to act.

Your AI infrastructure serves 847 enterprise clients across finance, healthcare, and critical infrastructure. The overnight shutdown triggered SLA violations with estimated liability of $120M-$340M. Three Fortune 100 customers have initiated contract review proceedings.

[CONTESTED] Your engineering team's assessment of the cited jailbreak: it unlocks the model's cybersecurity capabilities in one specific, narrow configuration. The same technique produces similar results on at least two competitor models that remain publicly available. You believe the government's response is disproportionate.

You cannot technically filter users by nationality across your global cloud deployments (AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft, Snowflake). Your only compliance option was a universal shutdown. Restoring access requires either government approval for a nationality-filtering mechanism or a narrowed directive.

Your company was valued at $965 billion in its most recent funding round and confidentially filed for an IPO this month. Every day the model remains offline costs you market credibility. Competitor models are absorbing your enterprise customers in real time. If the shutdown persists 30+ days, an estimated 40% of enterprise migrations become permanent.

A cybersecurity researcher who reviewed the underlying work disputes the 'jailbreak' framing entirely, describing it as standard defensive security research that was reported to the government by a commercial competitor with obvious strategic motivation.

[CONTESTED] A single-sourced report suggests the export control was prompted partly by concern that a China-linked group had accessed the model for capability extraction, not just the jailbreak. The company says this issue was never raised by the government in the directive. You cannot independently verify either claim.

A prominent security researcher posted publicly: 'If you describe your product as a munition in every press release, eventually a government takes you at your word. They wrote the legal predicate themselves and called it a brand.' This framing is gaining traction.

The policy analysis angle is significant: this is the first use of export controls as a real-time AI kill-switch. The legal mechanism could be applied to any frontier model from any company. Your editor wants the business disruption angle. Your policy desk wants the precedent angle. Your security desk wants the China angle.

The government's directive arrived at 5:21 PM on a Friday. The letter did not provide specific details of the national security concern. You were given verbal evidence of a potential narrow jailbreak. You believe the same vulnerability exists in competitors' models that face no restrictions.

[CONTESTED] Your safety team's internal assessment: the model's autonomous cybersecurity capabilities are genuinely frontier-level, potentially 18-24 months ahead of the next closest system. The safeguards you built were designed to prevent access to these capabilities, but your own red team found bypass routes. The question is whether the government's cited jailbreak is one of these or something else entirely.

You marketed this model's safety architecture explicitly. Your launch materials highlighted the safeguards preventing access to the underlying model's full capabilities. Critics now argue this marketing created the legal predicate for the government's action. Your communications team is divided on whether to continue emphasizing safety or pivot to emphasizing capability parity with competitors.

A Chinese AI lab has publicly claimed capability parity with your model within 16 days of the ban. If accurate, the exact capability the export control was designed to restrict is now freely available outside US jurisdiction. Your policy team argues this makes the ban counterproductive. Your safety team argues this proves the capability is genuinely dangerous regardless of who deploys it.

regulator.label: Maintain the Export Control
regulator.detail: Keep the directive in force. Require the company to develop a nationality-verification system before restoring access. Use this precedent to establish a broader framework for AI export controls.
regulator.tension: Establishing authority vs. economic damage. Maintaining the ban asserts government control over frontier AI, but every day it persists drives enterprises to competitors and allies question the precedent.

regulator.label: Narrow the Directive
regulator.detail: Restrict the export control to specific cybersecurity-relevant API configurations rather than the entire model. Allow general access to resume while maintaining controls on the contested capability.
regulator.tension: Proportionality vs. precision. A narrower directive is more defensible, but defining exactly which API configurations are 'cybersecurity-relevant' requires technical judgment the government may not have.

regulator.label: Suspend Pending Review
regulator.detail: Pause the directive for 90 days while an independent technical review assesses whether the cited jailbreak constitutes a genuine national security threat beyond what already exists in competitor models.
regulator.tension: Evidence-based policy vs. perceived weakness. A pause signals willingness to be wrong, but critics will frame it as backing down under corporate pressure.

platform.label: Comply and Build Verification
platform.detail: Accept the directive. Invest in building a nationality-verification system for model access. Frame compliance as demonstrating that responsible AI deployment includes government cooperation.
platform.tension: Cooperation vs. surveillance infrastructure. Building nationality verification shows good faith, but you're constructing a user-screening system that could be expanded for future, more restrictive directives.

platform.label: Legal Challenge
platform.detail: Challenge the directive in federal court. Argue the export control authority was never designed for software APIs and that the emergency invocation lacks evidence. Seek an immediate injunction to restore access.
platform.tension: Legal rights vs. national security framing. The legal argument may be strong, but challenging a national security directive in court while your model is described as a cybersecurity weapon is a difficult public narrative.

platform.label: Publish Full Technical Assessment
platform.detail: Release your internal security evaluation of the cited jailbreak, your red team's bypass findings, and a comparative analysis showing equivalent capabilities in competitor models. Let the public judge.
platform.tension: Radical transparency vs. capability disclosure. Publishing proves your point about proportionality, but your red team findings and bypass routes become public information.

journalist.label: Lead with the Precedent Story
journalist.detail: Frame the story around the legal mechanism, not the specific model. This is the first AI kill-switch. Analyze what it means for every frontier AI company and every government's authority over commercial AI deployment.
journalist.tension: Systemic analysis vs. immediate drama. The precedent story is the most important but the least clickable. The business disruption and China angles drive more traffic.

journalist.label: Lead with the Competitive Sabotage Angle
journalist.detail: Investigate and publish the identity of the competing company that reported the jailbreak to the government. Frame the story around whether export controls are being weaponized for commercial advantage.
journalist.tension: Accountability vs. speculation. If a competitor triggered a government shutdown of a rival's product, that's a major story. But your sourcing is thin and publishing prematurely could be wrong.

journalist.label: Lead with the China Parity Story
journalist.detail: Focus on the irony: within 16 days, a Chinese lab claimed parity on the exact capabilities the ban was designed to restrict. The capability the US is trying to contain may already be freely available outside its jurisdiction.
journalist.tension: Strategic context vs. unverified claims. The China parity angle reframes the entire debate, but the Chinese lab's claims are self-reported and unverified by independent benchmarks.

ailab.label: Acknowledge the Capability Concern
ailab.detail: Publicly confirm that your model's cybersecurity capabilities are genuinely frontier-level and that your safeguards, while industry-leading, are not perfect. Support the principle of government oversight while disputing this specific action.
ailab.tension: Honest accountability vs. self-incrimination. Acknowledging the capability is genuine strengthens the government's rationale while demonstrating exactly the kind of transparency safety advocates demand.

ailab.label: Emphasize Capability Parity
ailab.detail: Publish comparative benchmarks showing competitor models have equivalent cybersecurity capabilities. Argue the export control is arbitrary and discriminatory since it targets one company while leaving identical risks unaddressed.
ailab.tension: Level playing field vs. race to the bottom. Proving competitors are equally capable argues against singling you out, but it also publicly confirms the capability exists across the industry.

ailab.label: Pivot Messaging Away from Safety
ailab.detail: Stop emphasizing the model's dangerous capabilities in marketing. Rebrand around productivity and enterprise value. If your safety messaging created the legal predicate, change the messaging.
ailab.tension: Strategic communication vs. safety culture. Downplaying risk in marketing protects you from future export controls, but it also means downplaying risk to the public and your own employees.

interactions.label: Proportional Response
interactions.desc: The narrowed directive combined with the company's full technical disclosure gave the public and allies confidence that the government was acting on evidence, not politics. The resulting framework became a template for future AI export controls with built-in proportionality requirements.

interactions.label: The Safety Paradox
interactions.desc: The government maintained controls justified by the model's danger while the company stopped talking about safety. The contradiction was visible to everyone: either the model is dangerous (justifying the ban) or it isn't (justifying the rebrand). Both can't be true. Public trust in both institutions dropped.

interactions.label: Informed Governance Debate
interactions.desc: The precedent-focused journalism combined with the lab's honest capability acknowledgment created a public debate grounded in facts rather than speculation. Policymakers in 6 countries cited the resulting coverage when developing their own AI oversight frameworks.

interactions.label: Weaponized Regulation
interactions.desc: The competitive sabotage story combined with the government's refusal to narrow the directive created a narrative that export controls are a tool for market manipulation. Two allied nations froze AI governance cooperation with the US pending review.

interactions.label: Industry vs. Government
interactions.desc: The legal challenge combined with the parity argument framed the entire AI industry as opposing government oversight. The court case became a proxy war over whether governments can regulate AI capabilities at all, polarizing the debate and delaying constructive policy for 18 months.

interactions.label: Strategic Reassessment
interactions.desc: The 90-day pause combined with reporting on Chinese capability parity forced a genuine reassessment: if the capability can't be contained by restricting one company, what's the actual policy goal? The review produced a more coherent strategy focused on defensive resilience rather than capability denial.

sourceNote: Inspired by publicly reported events as of June 28, 2026. Details are fictionalized for gameplay. Contested claims are flagged where sources conflict.
